A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities and countries that work together to deliver websites, videos, and images faster. Without one, every request for a webpage would travel all the way back to a single origin server — the original computer where a website's files are permanently stored — no matter how far away the visitor happens to be. That long trip takes time and can cause slow loading, especially during busy periods or for people located far from that server.

To fix this, copies of a website's files get stored on many smaller computers placed closer to visitors around the world. Each of these nearby computers is called an edge location, since it sits at the "edge" of the network, near the people using it rather than at the distant center. When someone requests a page and the nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that success is called a cache hit, meaning the answer came from a local copy instead of a long trip to the origin server. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries holding copies of popular books, so readers rarely need to travel to the one faraway central library that owns the sole master copy. This arrangement makes browsing feel quicker, reduces strain on the origin server, and keeps things working smoothly even when many people request the same content at once, anywhere in the world.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's master files | Everything ultimately comes from here if no closer copy exists |
| Edge location | A nearby computer holding copies of popular content | Shortens the distance data must travel to reach a visitor |
| Cache hit | A request answered by a stored copy instead of the origin | Speeds up loading and reduces load on the origin server |
| Latency | The delay caused by distance and network travel time | Lower latency means pages and videos feel faster to use |
